lessons.title: Common Faults and Diagnostic Techniques
lessons.body:
When your solar pump stops working, start with the simplest checks. First, look at the controller display. Many controllers show error codes like E01 for low voltage or E04 for dry run. Write down the code and check the manual. If there is no display, use a multimeter to measure the voltage at the pump terminals. A 24V system should read between 26V and 30V in full sun. If it reads below 22V, the problem is likely in the array or wiring.

Next, check the water source. A clogged intake screen or a fallen dam level can cause the pump to run dry. Remove the pump from the dam and inspect the intake. Clean any mud, leaves, or debris. In many African dams, silt builds up quickly during the rainy season, so check monthly. Also, listen to the pump. A humming sound without water flow often means a stuck impeller or a broken shaft. A grinding noise points to worn bearings.

Use a clamp meter to measure current. For a 1kW pump, expect around 4A at 250V DC. If current is zero, you have an open circuit. If current is very high, you have a short or a seized pump. Check all connections for corrosion. In humid areas, terminals corrode fast. Clean them with sandpaper and apply petroleum jelly. Test the float switch or pressure switch with a multimeter in continuity mode. A faulty switch is a common fault.

Finally, check the solar array. Look for shadows from trees or dust. Even a small shadow on one panel can cut output by 50%. Clean panels with a soft cloth and water. Measure open-circuit voltage of each panel. A 250W panel should read about 37V open-circuit. If one panel reads much lower, it is faulty. By following these steps, you can find most faults in under an hour.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Low Water Output
lessons.body:
If your pump runs but delivers less water than before, first measure the actual flow. Use a bucket and a stopwatch. For example, if you expect 10,000 litres per day but only get 4,000, you have a problem. Check the sun conditions. A cloudy day can reduce output by 70%. Compare with a sunny day. If output is still low, check the array tilt. Panels should face north in the southern hemisphere (most of Africa) and be tilted at an angle equal to your latitude. For Nairobi (1Â°S), tilt 5-10Â°; for Johannesburg (26Â°S), tilt 26Â°. A wrong tilt can cut daily output by 20-30%.

Next, inspect the pump intake and impeller. Sand and silt wear impellers quickly. Remove the pump and open the pump end. If impeller blades are worn thin or broken, replace them. In many African dams, fine clay particles act like sandpaper. Install a sediment trap or a pre-filter. Also, check for leaks in the pipes. A small leak on the suction side can suck air and reduce flow. Tighten all joints and replace cracked pipes. Use a pressure gauge to check for blockages. A clogged filter or non-return valve can restrict flow.

Check the controller settings. Some controllers have a maximum power point tracking (MPPT) setting that may be off. Reset to factory defaults or adjust according to the manual. If the controller has a speed setting, ensure it is at 100%. Also, verify that the float switch is not stuck in a partially closed position. Test by bypassing the switch temporarily. If flow increases, replace the switch.

Finally, measure the voltage and current at the pump while running. If voltage is low (below 200V for a 240V system), the array is undersized or there is voltage drop in the cables. Use thicker cables for long runs. For a 50m run at 10A, use at least 6mmÂ² copper cable. If current is low but voltage is normal, the pump may be worn. In that case, replace the pump end or the whole pump. Regular maintenance every 6 months prevents most low-output problems.

lessons.title: Electrical Fault Finding: Open Circuits, Shorts, Ground Faults
lessons.body:
Electrical faults stop pumps dead. You need a digital multimeter and a clamp meter. Start by isolating the array from the controller. Measure the open-circuit voltage (Voc) of the array. For a 24V system, Voc should be around 44V for two 250W panels in series. If Voc is zero, you have an open circuit. Check each panel individually. A broken wire or a blown fuse is common. Look for rodent damageârats love to chew DC cables. Repair with proper MC4 connectors and heat-shrink tubing.

If Voc is normal but the pump does not run, check for a short circuit. Set your multimeter to continuity or resistance mode. With the array disconnected, measure resistance between the positive and negative cables at the controller. It should read infinite (open). If it reads near zero, you have a short. Trace the cables and look for pinched or cut insulation. In dam environments, water can enter junction boxes and cause shorts. Seal all boxes with silicone and use IP68 connectors.

Ground faults are dangerous. Measure resistance between the positive cable and earth ground (a metal stake in the ground). It should be infinite. If you read any resistance, you have a ground fault. This often happens when a cable is damaged and touches the metal pump housing or a wet surface. Disconnect the pump and test again. If the fault disappears, the pump motor is grounded. Replace the pump. If the fault remains, the cable is damaged. Use a megohmmeter (insulation tester) for better accuracy. A good reading is above 1 megohm.

Also, check the controller's internal fuses. Many controllers have a 20A fuse. Test with a multimeter. A blown fuse indicates a short or overload. Never replace with a higher rating. After fixing a fault, test the system with a low-voltage source first, like a 12V battery, to avoid damaging the controller. Always turn off the array before working on wiring. In Africa, many faults come from poor connections due to heat and humidity. Use dielectric grease on all terminals and re-tighten every 6 months.

lessons.title: Pump Performance Degradation and Solutions
lessons.body:
Over time, every pump loses performance. A new pump might deliver 20,000 litres per day; after two years, it might only give 12,000. The main causes are wear, corrosion, and scaling. In African dams, water often contains sand, silt, and minerals. These act like sandpaper on impellers and seals. First, measure the pump's flow and head. Use a pressure gauge at the outlet and a bucket to measure flow. Compare with the pump's original curve. If flow is down by more than 20%, it's time for maintenance.

Open the pump and inspect the impeller. Worn impellers have rounded edges or cracks. Replace the impeller and wear rings. For a typical 1kW pump, an impeller kit costs $50-$100. Also, check the mechanical seal. A leaking seal lets water into the motor, causing rust and short circuits. Replace seals every 2 years. In sandy water, use a silicon carbide seal for longer life. Clean the motor windings with electrical contact cleaner and dry them in the sun before reassembly.

Scaling from calcium and magnesium is common in boreholes and some dams. Scale reduces the impeller clearance and blocks cooling passages. Descale with a weak acid solution (5% citric acid) for 30 minutes, then rinse. Never use strong acid. For solar pumps, also check the controller's maximum power point tracking. If the controller is old, it may not track well. Upgrading to a modern MPPT controller can recover 10-15% of lost output. Also, check the array for degradation. Solar panels lose about 0.5% per year. After 10 years, a 250W panel might only produce 230W. Clean panels regularly and replace any with cracked glass or discoloration.

Finally, adjust the pump's operating point. If the dam level has dropped, the pump may be running at a higher head, reducing flow. Lower the pump or add a booster pump. For a dam, use a floating pump or a submersible on a adjustable stand. Regular maintenance every 6 monthsâcleaning, tightening, and lubricatingâcan double the pump's life. Keep a log of flow and pressure to spot degradation early.

lessons.title: Optimizing Array Tilt and Orientation
lessons.body:
Solar panels make most power when sunlight hits them straight on. In Africa, the sun is always in the north for southern hemisphere countries, and in the south for northern hemisphere countries. For most of sub-Saharan Africa, panels should face north. The correct tilt angle is your latitude. For Nairobi (1Â°S), tilt 5-10Â°; for Harare (17Â°S), tilt 17Â°; for Cape Town (34Â°S), tilt 34Â°. If you are in West Africa, like Ghana (8Â°N), face south and tilt 8Â°. A wrong orientation can cut daily output by 20-40%.

You can adjust tilt seasonally. In summer, the sun is higher, so use a lower tilt (latitude minus 10Â°). In winter, use a higher tilt (latitude plus 10Â°). For a fixed system, set tilt at latitude. But if you rely on the pump year-round, seasonal adjustment gives up to 15% more water. Use a simple inclinometer or a smartphone app to measure tilt. Mark the frame with paint so you can return to the same angle. For a dam pump, you may need to mount panels on a ground rack, not on a roof, to allow adjustment.

Avoid shading at all costs. Even a small shadow from a tree branch or a pole can drop output by 50%. In the morning and afternoon, shadows are long. Walk around your array at 9am, noon, and 3pm. Cut any trees or move the array. Also, clean panels weekly in dusty areas. Dust from the Sahel can reduce output by 1% per day if not cleaned. Use a soft brush and water. Never clean hot panels with cold waterâthey can crack.

For a dam pump, you can also use a tracking system. A single-axis tracker follows the sun east to west and can increase output by 25-30%. But trackers cost more and need maintenance. For small systems, manual adjustment is cheaper. If you have multiple panels, wire them in series to match the controller's voltage. For a 24V system, use two 250W panels in series. For a 48V system, use four. Always check the controller's maximum input voltage. In Africa, high temperatures reduce panel voltage by about 0.4% per Â°C. So a 250W panel rated at 37V might only give 33V at 50Â°C. Account for this when sizing cables and controllers.

lessons.title: Data Logging and Performance Analysis
lessons.body:
You cannot improve what you do not measure. Start a simple logbook. Every day, write down: date, time, weather (sunny, cloudy, rainy), water output (litres), pump run hours, and any error codes. Use a 1-litre jug to calibrate a larger container. For example, fill a 200-litre drum and time it. Then you can estimate daily output. If you have a flow meter, even better. A basic mechanical flow meter costs $30 and fits in the pipe. Record the reading at the start and end of each day.

For electrical data, use a cheap data logger. A USB voltage and current logger costs $50. Connect it between the array and controller. It will record voltage, current, and power every minute. Download the data weekly to a laptop or phone. Look for patterns. If power drops every afternoon, it might be due to shading or a hot controller. If voltage is low in the morning, the array may be undersized. Compare daily energy (watt-hours) with water output. A good system might use 5 kWh to pump 20,000 litres. If energy is high but water is low, the pump is inefficient.

Analyze your data monthly. Calculate the performance ratio: actual water output divided by expected output. Expected output = (array power Ã peak sun hours Ã pump efficiency) / (head Ã 9.81). For a 1kW array, 5 peak sun hours, 50% efficiency, and 20m head, expected output = (1000 Ã 5 Ã 0.5) / (20 Ã 9.81) = 12.7 mÂ³/day. If you get 8 mÂ³, your performance ratio is 0.63. That means you are losing 37% to faults, dirt, or wrong tilt. Investigate the biggest losses first.

Use the data to schedule maintenance. If flow drops by 10% in a month, clean the panels and check the intake. If current spikes, check for a short. If voltage is low on sunny days, test each panel. Keep logs for at least a year to see seasonal changes. In Africa, the rainy season brings clouds and silt. Your log will tell you when to expect lower output. Share your data with other farmers. Rise Africa Skills can help you set up a simple Excel sheet or a free app like PumpLogger. With good data, you can optimize your system and avoid costly breakdowns.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check when a solar pump stops working?
options: B) Check the controller display for error codes
quiz.explanation: The controller often shows an error code that points to the fault.

quiz.q: A 24V solar pump system should read what voltage at the pump terminals in full sun?
quiz.explanation: A healthy 24V system runs between 26V and 30V under full sun.

quiz.q: What tool is used to measure current in a solar pump circuit?
quiz.explanation: A clamp meter measures current without breaking the circuit.

quiz.q: A grinding noise from the pump usually indicates:
quiz.explanation: Grinding is a classic sign of worn bearings or a damaged shaft.

quiz.q: How often should you check the pump intake screen in a dam with silt?
quiz.explanation: Silt builds up quickly, so monthly checks prevent clogging.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of low water output from a solar pump?
quiz.explanation: Incorrect tilt reduces daily solar energy and thus water output.

quiz.q: For a location at 26Â°S latitude, what is the correct fixed tilt for solar panels?
quiz.explanation: Fixed tilt should equal the latitude for year-round performance.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean a clogged intake screen?
quiz.explanation: A soft brush and water remove debris without damaging the screen.

quiz.q: A small leak on the suction side of a pump can cause:
options: B) Air entering and reduced flow
quiz.explanation: Air leaks reduce pumping efficiency and can cause cavitation.

quiz.q: What is the expected open-circuit voltage (Voc) of a 250W solar panel?
quiz.explanation: A typical 250W panel has a Voc around 37V.

quiz.q: If the array voltage is zero, what is the likely fault?
quiz.explanation: Zero voltage means the circuit is broken somewhere.

quiz.q: What should resistance between positive and negative cables at the controller read when the array is disconnected?
quiz.explanation: A healthy circuit shows infinite resistance (open circuit).

quiz.q: A ground fault is detected when resistance between positive cable and earth is:
quiz.explanation: Any measurable resistance to ground indicates a fault.

quiz.q: What is the best tool to check insulation resistance?
quiz.explanation: A megohmmeter applies high voltage to test insulation.

quiz.q: What should you do before working on solar array wiring?
quiz.explanation: Always disconnect the array to avoid electric shock.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of pump performance degradation over time?
quiz.explanation: Impeller wear from sand and silt reduces flow.

quiz.q: How often should mechanical seals be replaced in a sandy water pump?
quiz.explanation: Seals wear out; every 2 years is a safe interval.

quiz.q: What chemical can be used to descale a pump impeller?
quiz.explanation: Weak citric acid safely dissolves mineral scale.

quiz.q: Upgrading to a modern MPPT controller can recover what percentage of lost output?
quiz.explanation: MPPT controllers improve energy harvesting by 10-15%.

quiz.q: Solar panels typically lose what percentage of output per year?
quiz.explanation: Panel degradation is about 0.5% per year.

quiz.q: For a location at 17Â°S latitude, what is the correct fixed tilt?
quiz.explanation: Fixed tilt should equal the latitude.

quiz.q: What is the effect of a small shadow on one solar panel?
quiz.explanation: Shading one panel can reduce string output by up to 50%.

quiz.q: How often should you clean solar panels in dusty areas?
quiz.explanation: Dust can reduce output by 1% per day, so weekly cleaning is best.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a single-axis tracker?
quiz.explanation: Trackers follow the sun and increase output by 25-30%.

quiz.q: What should you record daily in a pump logbook?
quiz.explanation: Daily logs of output and weather help spot trends.

quiz.q: What does a performance ratio of 0.63 mean?
quiz.explanation: Performance ratio is actual divided by expected output.

quiz.q: What is a cheap tool to measure water flow?
quiz.explanation: A bucket and stopwatch give a simple flow measurement.

quiz.q: If power drops every afternoon, what is a likely cause?
quiz.explanation: Afternoon drops can be from shading, heat, or lower sun angle.

quiz.q: What should you do if flow drops by 10% in a month?
options: B) Clean panels and check intake
quiz.explanation: A 10% drop often indicates dirt or a clogged intake.

quiz.q: Why keep logs for at least a year?
quiz.explanation: Seasonal patterns help predict and prevent problems.
